title: How do you reverse an integer array without using any inbuilt functions?
shortTitle: Reverse an integer array without using inbuilt functions

s1_definition.profdef: Swap elements from both ends moving inward: `arr[0]↔arr[n-1]`, `arr[1]↔arr[n-2]`, until pointers meet in the middle. Time: O(n/2) = O(n). Space: O(1) — in-place. No Collections.reverse(), no Arrays, no streams. Pure two-pointer swap. Stream approach (not in-place): `IntStream.range(0,n).map(i -> arr[n-1-i]).toArray()`.
s1_definition.analogy: Transaction IDs [001, 002, 003, 004, 005] → reversed [005, 004, 003, 002, 001]. Like flipping a stack of cheques: swap top and bottom, then second and second-to-last, continue until middle.
s1_definition.oneliner: Two pointers: left=0, right=n-1. Swap arr[left]↔arr[right]. left++, right--. Stop when left >= right. O(n) time, O(1) space.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Swap elements from both ends moving inward: `arr[0]↔arr[n-1]`, `arr[1]↔arr[n-2]`, until pointers meet in the middle. Time: O(n/2) = O(n). Space: O(1) — in-place. No Collections.reverse(), no Arrays, no streams. Pure two-pointer swap. Stream approach (not in-place): `IntStream.range(0,n).map(i -> arr[n-1-i]).toArray()`.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Transaction IDs [001, 002, 003, 004, 005] → reversed [005, 004, 003, 002, 001]. Like flipping a stack of cheques: swap top and bottom, then second and second-to-last, continue until middle.

**One line to remember:** Two pointers: left=0, right=n-1. Swap arr[left]↔arr[right]. left++, right--. Stop when left >= right. O(n) time, O(1) space.

sections.s2_technical:
Reversing an integer array without a library reverse method can still use streams by driving an `IntStream` of indices from the end. The idiom is `IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n).map(i -> arr[n - i]).toArray()`, which reads each element from the back and builds a new array. No `Collections.reverse` or `StringBuilder.reverse` is used.

`IntStream.rangeClosed(1, n)` produces indices 1..n without boxing. `map(i -> arr[n - i])` converts each index to the element counted from the end: for i=1 it takes `arr[n-1]` (the last), for i=n it takes `arr[0]` (the first). `toArray()` materialises the reversed primitive array. Because it writes to a NEW array, the source is not mutated.

A banking example: a ledger stores end-of-day balances oldest-first, but a statement must show newest-first. The index-mapping reverse produces the display order without altering the stored ledger. Senior nuance: using primitive `IntStream` avoids autoboxing every element into `Integer`, which matters for large ledgers.
sections.s3_banking: Problem — The ledger stored daily balances oldest-first, but customer statements must display newest-first, and mutating the stored array risked corrupting the audit record. Fix: an `IntStream` of reversed indices maps each position to `arr[n-i]` and builds a NEW reversed array, leaving the ledger intact.

sections.s5_journey:
**Step 1.** Input: balances [100, 200, 300, 400], length n=4.

**Step 2.** `IntStream.rangeClosed(1, 4)` produces 1,2,3,4 with no boxing.

**Step 3.** `map(i -> balances[4 - i])` reads from the end: i=1→balances[3]=400, i=2→300, i=3→200, i=4→100.

**Step 4.** `toArray()` writes these into a NEW primitive array.

**Step 5.** The reversed array [400, 300, 200, 100] is returned; the source stays [100, 200, 300, 400].

```text
INFO: reversed=[400, 300, 200, 100] source unchanged
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│ Two-pointer swap (reverse cheque-number array)           │
│───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ int[] ids = {101,102,103,104,105};                       │
│ int left = 0, right = ids.length - 1;                    │
│ while (left < right) {                                   │
│     int tmp   = ids[left];                               │
│     ids[left] = ids[right];                              │
│     ids[right]= tmp;                                     │
│     left++; right--;                                     │
│ }                                                        │
├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│ Non-destructive stream variant (new array)              │
│───────────────────────────────────────────────────────── │
│ int n = ids.length;                                      │
│ int[] rev = IntStream.range(0, n)                        │
│     .map(i -> ids[n - 1 - i])                            │
│     .toArray();                                          │
│ // in-place = O(1) space (mutates original);            │
│ // stream    = O(n) extra space (keeps original intact) │
│ Pick in-place for large ledgers to avoid extra alloc.   │
└─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Reverse an array in-place with two pointers: left starts at 0, right at length-1. Swap arr[left] and arr[right], increment left, decrement right. Stop when left >= right. O(n) time, O(1) space. No inbuilt functions used. The middle element (odd-length array) stays in place — the pointers meet AT the middle.
